title: The eruv
hookLine: a symbolic boundary that turns a neighborhood into one shared home for Shabbat

cards: On some street corners, if you look up, you might spot it. Two poles, and a thin wire running across the top, then on down the block. You could walk under it every day and never notice.

It holds up no sign and carries no power. But to a family on Shabbat morning, that wire decides whether they can push a stroller to synagogue, carry a house key in a pocket, or bring a dish to a neighbor's lunch.

teach.b: Eruv. Start with yesterday's last father: carrying from one domain to another. Inside your own home you can carry on Shabbat.
Out in the public domain, or from a private space into a public one, you can't.
The rabbis tie that rule to the Torah's words, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day."
So a key, a book, a baby who can't walk yet: all of it stays inside. The rabbis didn't erase that rule. They asked a different question: what is a home?
First, a home is shared food. In the Mishnah's tractate Eruvin, the families around a shared courtyard each put in some food, kept together in one house.
Now they're one household eating from one table, and the courtyard is theirs.
Second, a home has doorways. The Talmud says two posts with a crosspiece over them count as the form of a doorway.
Run that doorway around a neighborhood, pole to pole, wire across the top, and the space inside can be treated as one enclosure.

teach.h: A HOME HAS TO BE KEPT.
teach.b: Third, a home has to be kept.
Communities that rely on an eruv check it before Shabbat, because a broken wire can mean it doesn't hold that week. And not every community uses one.

Some Orthodox authorities are strict about which eruvin they rely on, and Jews who don't keep the carrying rules have no need for one. The law about staying in your place is honored, and the neighbors become one place.

how: In some Jewish neighborhoods a community builds an eruv of poles and wire, checks it each week before Shabbat and announces whether it is up; families who rely on it then carry within it on Shabbat. Others who keep the carrying rules carry nothing outside without one.

games.q: you share a courtyard with three other families. on Shabbat you want to carry a dish from your door to your neighbor's. what do you do?
o: carry it anyway; it's only a few steps.
before Shabbat, all the families put food together in one house.
leave the dish at home and stay hungry.
games.why: the Mishnah's answer is shared food. pooled in one house, it makes the families one household, and the courtyard becomes theirs to carry in.

practice: Picture the few homes closest to yours, on either side, above, below, across: a name if you know it, a face if you don't.
Now picture a thin line running around all of you, turning the street into one house, and notice who's inside it with you.

wordCard.voice: Eruv. A shared meal and a boundary of poles and wire that let a whole neighborhood count as one home for carrying on Shabbat. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the arrangement that joins households or spaces into one for Shabbat.
